story.title: Nepali Hydropower Worker Survives 10 Days in Flooded Tunnel
story.summary: Sanjay Sah, a Nepali hydropower worker, survived for 10 days in a flooded tunnel after a flash flood struck the China-Nepal border on August 26. During his ordeal, he drank muddy water and lost track of time while praying for rescue. He was eventually rescued on September 4, amidst a disaster that resulted in at least 1,429 fatalities and left over 5,640 people missing.

explore_lenses.label: Why were hydropower workers so exposed?
explore_lenses.title: Floodwater rapidly cut off underground exits
explore_lenses.summary: Sah’s account indicates workers received a warning but had only minutes before the tunnel flooded. The disaster exposed how debris-filled underground works and damaged access roads can turn a flood into a prolonged rescue emergency.

claims.text: Sah said workers were warned that a major flood was approaching and tried to shut down equipment and evacuate colleagues, but the water gave them too little time; the tunnel was engulfed within minutes.
Local reporting said Sah remained behind to help dozens of colleagues leave the Trishuli 3A project, losing his own opportunity to escape.

Rescuers reported that mud, boulders, collapsed passages and damaged roads were obstructing access to hydropower tunnels; at least 900 workers across a dozen projects were reported missing, with roughly 500 believed to be underground at the time of the report.

explore_lenses.uncertainty_note: The precise number and locations of workers still trapped or killed in individual tunnels remained unclear as searches and identifications continued.

explore_lenses.label: What caused the catastrophic flood?
explore_lenses.title: The initiating collapse is under investigation
explore_lenses.summary: Reporting describes a high-mountain collapse involving ice and rock near the border, but Nepal’s government said the event’s causes and evolution were still being studied. That distinction matters because a description of the physical event is not yet a completed finding on its trigger or preventability.

claims.text: Nepal’s foreign minister said on September 3 that the government was continuing technical study of the causes and evolution of the August 26 event.

Associated Press reported that researchers believed a high-altitude slope collapse involving rock and glacial ice sent debris downstream, while cautioning against drawing a direct causal line to climate change.
Sah described several-metre, tsunami-like waves and said workers had received an alert, but his account does not establish why the collapse or flood occurred.

explore_lenses.label: What happens after the tunnel rescue?
explore_lenses.title: Search, identification and reconstruction continue
explore_lenses.summary: Sah’s rescue did not end the emergency: teams were still searching tunnels and identifying remains, while the government faced extensive infrastructure recovery needs. Nepal has sought specialized foreign assistance for both rescue and forensic work.

claims.text: Nepal said specialized tunnel-rescue teams from India, China and South Korea were working with the Nepali Army at named hydropower sites, while additional equipment and logistical support were arriving.

The government said forensic teams from India, China, Singapore and South Korea were assisting Nepal Police with identifying recovered remains, including through DNA collection before temporary burial where necessary.

Sah urged authorities to continue searching for survivors or recover bodies for families; reporting said a Chinese worker was rescued on September 5, but no further signs of life had been heard by September 13.

Forecast: Reconstruction will place substantial pressure on Nepal’s finances; disaster authorities’ preliminary damage estimate was reported as $2.56 billion, while the final rebuilding cost had not been calculated.

story_report.summary: Nepali hydropower worker Sanjay Sah was rescued on September 4 after surviving 10 days in a flooded tunnel following the August 26 flash flood. His escape was followed by the rescue of a Chinese worker the next day, though no further signs of life had been heard by September 13. The wider disaster had killed at least 1,429 people and left more than 5,640 missing.

sections.heading: Warnings and obstacles at hydropower tunnels
sections.body: Sah said workers were warned that a major flood was approaching and tried to shut down equipment and evacuate colleagues, but water engulfed the tunnel within minutes. Local reporting said he remained behind to help dozens of colleagues leave the Trishuli 3A project, losing his own chance to escape. Rescue access was obstructed by mud, boulders, collapsed passages and damaged roads; reports put at least 900 workers missing across a dozen projects, with roughly 500 believed to have been underground.

sections.heading: Investigators assess the flood's origins
sections.body: Nepal’s foreign minister said on September 3 that the government was continuing technical study of the event’s causes and evolution. Associated Press reported that researchers believed a high-altitude slope collapse involving rock and glacial ice had sent debris downstream, while cautioning that this did not establish a direct link to climate change. Sah described several-metre, tsunami-like waves, but his account did not establish what caused the collapse or flooding.

sections.heading: International teams support recovery operations
sections.body: Nepal said specialized tunnel-rescue teams from India, China and South Korea were working with the Nepali Army at hydropower sites, with additional equipment and logistical support arriving. Forensic teams from India, China, Singapore and South Korea were also assisting Nepal Police to identify recovered remains, including through DNA collection before temporary burial where needed. Reconstruction is expected to strain Nepal’s finances: preliminary damage was estimated at $2.56 billion, while the final rebuilding cost had not been calculated.

related_stories.title: Rescue Efforts Ongoing After Indonesian Ferry Capsizes, Leaving Six Dead and 130 Missing
related_stories.summary: A ferry named Virgo Transport 8 capsized in the Java Sea during bad weather, resulting in at least six confirmed deaths and approximately 130 people missing. The vessel was carrying 243 individuals, including crew members, when it lost contact with its operator. Rescue operations have successfully located 107 survivors, while search efforts continue for those unaccounted for.

related_stories.title: Turkish Police Detain Dozens in Crackdown on LGBTQ+ Community
related_stories.summary: In a recent crackdown, Turkish authorities have detained at least 162 individuals during raids on gay bars and the homes of LGBTQ+ activists. The government claims these actions are part of a campaign to uphold traditional family values. Additionally, more than a dozen accounts belonging to Turkish LGBTQ organizations have been blocked on social media at the request of authorities.

related_stories.summary: King Oyo Nyimba of the Tooro Kingdom was buried in western Uganda amid a contentious succession dispute. His death at the age of 34 has led to speculation about potential heirs, including rumors of illegitimate offspring, complicating the search for a successor.

related_stories.summary: A ferry capsized off the coast of Java, Indonesia, resulting in six confirmed fatalities and 129 individuals reported missing. The national search and rescue agency, Basarnas, has successfully rescued 108 people as efforts continue to locate those unaccounted for.
